headings.title: Introduction and Overview of Intrauterine Devices (IUDs)
headings.content: An intrauterine device (IUD) is a small, T-shaped plastic device that is inserted into the uterine cavity by a trained healthcare provider to provide safe, highly effective, and reversible long-acting reversible contraception (LARC). For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding the role of IUDs is crucial, as they are a cornerstone of family planning services promoted by the Federal Ministry of Health to reduce maternal mortality and manage population growth. IUDs are categorized primarily into copper-bearing devices and hormonal systems. They appeal to many clients because once inserted, they offer continuous protection for several years without requiring daily compliance or user action. As nursing professionals, we play a vital role in dispelling local myths regarding IUDs—such as the misconception that they cause infertility or migrate to the heart—and providing evidence-based counseling to prospective users. The procedure requires strict aseptic technique, careful bimanual examination, and comprehensive client assessment to ensure suitability. By mastering the fundamentals of IUD provision, Nigerian nurses empower women and families to make informed reproductive choices, thereby contributing significantly to community health outcomes and achieving national demographic goals.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Action of Copper and Hormonal IUDs
headings.content: The mechanism of action of intrauterine devices depends largely on whether the device is copper-bearing or hormonal. Copper IUDs, such as the TCu380A, release copper ions into the uterine cavity. These ions create a sterile, inflammatory reaction that is toxic to spermatozoa and ova, significantly impairing sperm motility, viability, and capacitation, thereby preventing fertilization. Additionally, the local endometrial environment is altered, making it hostile to implantation should fertilization somehow occur. On the other hand, hormonal IUDs release a progestin, such as levonorgestrel, directly into the uterine cavity. This local hormone action thickens the cervical mucus, which creates a formidable physical barrier preventing sperm penetration into the upper reproductive tract. Furthermore, levonorgestrel suppresses the endometrium, causing it to atrophy and become thin, which prevents blastocyst implantation and also explains why users often experience significantly lighter menstrual bleeding or amenorrhea. Understanding these distinct cellular and physiological pathways allows nurses to accurately counsel clients on what to expect regarding changes to their menstrual patterns, reassuring them that these localized actions do not disrupt systemic ovulation in the case of copper devices or cause widespread systemic side effects compared to oral contraceptive pills.

headings.title: Types of IUDs Available in Nigerian Healthcare Settings
headings.content: In Nigerian healthcare settings, the availability of specific IUD types is often guided by the National Drug Policy, public health procurement programs, and donor-supported family planning initiatives. The most widely available and frequently utilized device in public clinics and primary health care centers is the copper-bearing TCu380A, which is valued for its high efficacy and long duration of use—approved for up to 12 years. Other variants like the Multiload copper IUD may also be encountered. Hormonal IUDs, such as the Mirena or newer levonorgestrel-releasing systems, are increasingly available, particularly in private hospitals, tertiary health institutions, and urban clinics, though their higher cost can limit accessibility for rural clients. As nurses, it is essential to be familiar with the physical characteristics, insertion kits, and specific lifespans of the brands available in your facility. You must also educate clients on the approved duration of use for each specific device, ensuring that clients return for timely removal or replacement before the expiration date to avoid unintended pregnancies or device embedding. Navigating these options requires nurses to assess client preference, financial capacity, and clinical indications to recommend the most appropriate device.

headings.title: Client Selection, Contraindications, and Clinical Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical evaluation before IUD insertion is a critical nursing responsibility governed by the World Health Organization (WHO) Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraceptive use. Nurses must conduct a thorough health history to screen for absolute and relative contraindications, which include active pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), current pregnancy, unexplained abnormal uterine bleeding, gestational trophoblastic disease, and certain malignancies such as cervical or endometrial cancer. A comprehensive physical and pelvic examination must be performed, assessing for uterine size, position (anteverted or retroverted), and tenderness, as well as screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) like gonorrhea and chlamydia. If an STI or purulent cervical discharge is suspected, treatment must be initiated or ruled out before insertion to prevent introducing bacteria into the upper uterine cavity, which drastically increases the risk of PID. Nurses must also evaluate clients with a history of ectopic pregnancy, severe dysmenorrhea, or anatomical uterine abnormalities with heightened caution. By meticulously following these screening protocols, nurses safeguard clients against preventable complications and ensure that the chosen method is both safe and clinically appropriate for the individual woman.

headings.title: Nursing Procedures for IUD Insertion and Removal
headings.content: The insertion and removal of an IUD are delicate clinical procedures that require specialized nursing competence, strict aseptic technique, and gentle manipulation. Before starting, the nurse or midwife must explain the procedure step-by-step to gain the client's cooperation and alleviate anxiety. The procedure involves placing the client in the lithotomy position, performing a bimanual examination to determine uterine position, and inserting a bivalve speculum to visualize the cervix. The cervix is carefully cleansed with an antiseptic solution, and a tenaculum is gently placed on the anterior lip of the cervix to stabilize the uterus and straighten the uterocervical angle. A uterine sound is then gently introduced to measure the depth of the uterine cavity (usually between 6 to 9 cm). Following sounding, the loaded IUD is inserted using the withdrawal technique or specific manufacturer instructions, the arms are allowed to deploy, and the insertion tube is removed. Finally, the threads are trimmed, leaving about 2 to 3 cm visible in the vaginal vault. For removal, the client is placed in the lithotomy position, the speculum is inserted, and the threads are grasped gently with ring forceps, pulling outward with a steady, smooth traction. Nurses must monitor the client for vasovagal reactions, cramping, or hemorrhage throughout both procedures.

headings.title: Client Education, Follow-Up, and Management of Side Effects
headings.content: Comprehensive client education is essential for the long-term success and continuation of IUD use. Following insertion, nurses must inform clients to expect mild to moderate cramping and irregular spotting for the first few days to weeks, which can be managed with mild analgesics like ibuprofen. Clients must be taught how to check for the IUD threads by inserting clean fingers into the upper vagina, emphasizing that they should feel the strings but never pull on them. It is important to advise clients to return for a follow-up visit, typically after their first menses or 4 to 6 weeks post-insertion, to confirm that the device is still in place and that no infection has developed. Nurses should also discuss warning signs that require immediate medical evaluation, encapsulated in warning mnemonics like PAINS (Period late, Abdominal pain during intercourse, Infection signs, Not feeling well/fever, String missing or longer/shorter). Addressing common side effects—such as heavier bleeding with copper IUDs or amenorrhea with hormonal IUDs—reassures the client and prevents premature discontinuation driven by anxiety or misinformation. Empowering clients with this knowledge fosters adherence and ensures timely intervention should complications arise.

headings.title: Recognition and Management of IUD Complications
headings.content: While IUDs are exceptionally safe, nurses must be vigilant in recognizing and managing potential complications. Uterine perforation is a rare but serious complication that can occur during insertion if the sound or insertion tube breaches the myometrium, presenting with severe pelvic pain or loss of string visibility, requiring ultrasound imaging and possible surgical retrieval. Partial or complete expulsion occurs when the uterus pushes the IUD out into the cervical canal or vagina, often during heavy menstrual periods; if expelled, the client is no longer protected against pregnancy and requires a replacement or alternative method. Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can develop, particularly within the first 20 days post-insertion if pre-existing lower genital tract infections were undetected; this is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and removal of the IUD is typically recommended if the infection does not improve after 48 to 72 hours. Another concern is pregnancy with an IUD in situ; if pregnancy occurs, the nurse must facilitate an urgent ultrasound to rule out an ectopic pregnancy, and if the pregnancy is intrauterine, the clinician must assess whether to remove the IUD cautiously to reduce miscarriage risks. Early identification and prompt collaborative management by nursing and medical staff minimize morbidity and preserve the reproductive health of the client.
